movements.name: The GUI and the desktop metaphor
movements.summary: Windows, icons, menus and a pointer turned the computer into a picture of an office you could act on directly.

principles.name: Direct manipulation
principles.idea: Point at the thing and act on it, instead of typing a command that names it. The object on screen is the handle.
principles.example: Xerox Star 8010, drag a document icon onto the printer icon, 1981

principles.name: The metaphor as a teacher
principles.idea: Borrow a familiar world (desk, folder, trash) so a novice can predict what an action will do before trying it.
principles.example: Apple Macintosh Finder with folder and Trash icons, 1984

principles.name: What you see is what you get
principles.idea: The screen shows the printed result, so layout becomes something you see rather than something you encode.
principles.example: Gypsy editor on the Xerox Alto, Larry Tesler and Tim Mott, 1975

principles.name: Modelessness
principles.idea: The same gesture should mean the same thing everywhere; avoid hidden states that change what keys and clicks do.
principles.example: Cut, copy and paste as universal commands on the Apple Lisa, 1983

principles.name: Published consistency
principles.idea: Write the rules down so every application behaves alike; the guideline document is itself a design artefact.
principles.example: Human Interface Guidelines: The Apple Desktop Interface, 1987

keyWorks.title: NLS demonstration ('The Mother of All Demos')
Macintosh system icons and Chicago typeface
Human Interface Guidelines: The Apple Desktop Interface

movements.name: Computational design
movements.summary: Designers writing code as their material: type, layout and image generated by rules and responsive to data and time.

principles.name: Code is the material
principles.idea: The designer authors the rule that makes the form, not the form itself; changing a parameter is a design move.
principles.example: John Maeda, Design By Numbers, 1999

principles.name: Type in space and time
principles.idea: Text is not fixed on a page but zooms, layers and moves through depth, with hierarchy expressed by distance and focus.
principles.example: Muriel Cooper and the Visible Language Workshop, Information Landscapes, TED5, 1994

principles.name: A sketchbook for programmers
principles.idea: Make the tool small and immediate enough that a designer sketches in code the way they sketch in pencil.
principles.example: Processing, Casey Reas and Ben Fry, 2001

principles.name: Rules plus chance
principles.idea: Compose with constrained randomness so each run yields a new but related image; the system is the signature.
principles.example: Joshua Davis, praystation.com, Prix Ars Electronica Golden Nica, 2001

movements.name: Early web and Web 1.0
movements.summary: Hypertext before stylesheets: default grey pages, tables hacked into grids, animated GIFs, and artists treating the browser itself as material.

principles.name: The link is the layout
principles.idea: Navigation is a web of blue underlined words; structure lives in the connections between pages, not on a single page.
principles.example: Tim Berners-Lee, first public website at CERN, 1991

principles.name: Image inline with text
principles.idea: Once pictures could sit inside the text flow, the page became a graphic surface rather than a document.
principles.example: NCSA Mosaic 1.0, 1993

principles.name: Hack the medium
principles.idea: Coerce tools never meant for layout (tables, spacer GIFs, frames) into a grid; constraint becomes style.
principles.example: David Siegel, Creating Killer Web Sites, single-pixel GIF technique, 1996

principles.name: Vernacular authorship
principles.idea: Millions of amateurs publish with templates, counters, MIDI and under-construction signs; the amateur is the aesthetic.
principles.example: GeoCities neighbourhoods, from 1994

principles.name: The browser as subject
principles.idea: Artists expose the machinery (frames, source code, errors) instead of hiding it.
principles.example: Olia Lialina, My Boyfriend Came Back from the War, 1996

keyWorks.title: My Boyfriend Came Back from the War

movements.name: The Flash era
movements.summary: A vector plug-in let designers make the web move: intros, physics, generative toys and full-screen experiences outside HTML's limits.

principles.name: Motion as the primary medium
principles.idea: The site is a timeline; transitions, easing and choreography carry the brand more than static layout.
principles.example: Macromedia Flash 1.0 timeline-based authoring, 1996

principles.name: Physics instead of buttons
principles.idea: Interface elements behave like springs, liquids and swarms, so interaction feels like handling a material.
principles.example: Yugo Nakamura, ecotonoha for NEC, 2004

principles.name: Open the source
principles.idea: Share the working files so the community learns by dissecting; the source is part of the work.
principles.example: Joshua Davis, praystation.com open FLA files, 2001

principles.name: Time as content
principles.idea: A loop that runs forever (a clock, a dance) becomes the experience itself and a reason to leave the page open.
principles.example: Yugo Nakamura, UNIQLOCK for Uniqlo, 2007

keyWorks.title: Thoughts on Flash (Steve Jobs open letter)

movements.name: Y2K aesthetic
movements.summary: Translucent plastics, liquid chrome, blobs and techno-optimist sci-fi graphics around the millennium, revived by Gen Z in the 2020s.

principles.name: Translucency as candour
principles.idea: Show the insides through tinted plastic; the machine is friendly because you can see into it.
principles.example: Apple iMac G3 in Bondi Blue, 1998

principles.name: Liquid and chrome
principles.idea: Surfaces are glossy, reflective, bulbous, rendered rather than printed, signalling a digital future.
principles.example: Aqua interface preview at Macworld San Francisco, 2000

principles.name: Techno-graphic density
principles.idea: Layered pseudo-technical marks, codes and logotypes treat information graphics as decoration.
principles.example: The Designers Republic, Wipeout 2097 game graphics, 1996

movements.name: Skeuomorphism
movements.summary: Interfaces rendered as physical things (gel buttons, leather, felt, wood, paper) to make new software feel familiar and touchable.

principles.name: Familiarity through imitation
principles.idea: Dress a new function in the look of the object it replaces so users already know how to read it.
principles.example: iOS Notes on a yellow legal pad, iPhone OS 1.0, 2007

principles.name: Light and material as hierarchy
principles.idea: Gloss, bevel and shadow say which things are pressable and which are background.
principles.example: Aqua gel buttons and pinstriped windows, Mac OS X 10.0, 2001

principles.name: Touch needs affordance
principles.idea: On a glass screen with no physical keys, rendered depth substitutes for touch feedback.
principles.example: iPhone slide-to-unlock with a rendered slider, 2007

principles.name: Craft as brand
principles.idea: Lavish rendering signals care and premium quality, especially for apps sold on a store.
principles.example: Apple Podcasts reel-to-reel tape deck, iOS 6, 2012

movements.name: Flat design
movements.summary: Ornament stripped out: solid colour, type-led hierarchy and the grid return, a direct import of Swiss modernism into software.

principles.name: Authentically digital
principles.idea: Stop imitating physical objects; let the screen be a screen, with type, colour and motion native to it.
principles.example: Windows Phone 7 Metro interface, 2010

principles.name: Content over chrome
principles.idea: Shrink or remove frames, bars and borders so the content is the interface.
principles.example: Windows Phone 7 panorama hubs with oversized Segoe headings bleeding off-screen, 2010

principles.name: Type as hierarchy
principles.idea: Scale and weight of a single sans-serif carry structure that bevels and boxes used to carry.
principles.example: iOS 7 with Helvetica Neue Light, 2013

principles.name: Depth through layers, not texture
principles.idea: Translucent blurred panels and parallax give spatial order without rendering materials.
principles.example: iOS 7 Control Center blur, 2013

movements.name: Responsive web design
movements.summary: One layout that reflows across every screen using fluid grids, flexible images and media queries: the grid becomes a set of rules, not a fixed page.

principles.name: The fluid grid
principles.idea: Columns are proportions, not pixels; the grid stretches with the viewport.
principles.example: Ethan Marcotte, Responsive Web Design, A List Apart, 2010

principles.name: Breakpoints from content
principles.idea: Change the layout where the content breaks, not at named device widths.
principles.example: The Boston Globe responsive site, 2011

principles.name: Mobile first
principles.idea: Design the narrowest, most constrained version first and enhance upward, which forces prioritisation.
principles.example: Luke Wroblewski, Mobile First, 2011

principles.name: Intrinsic layout
principles.idea: Let elements size from their content with grid and flex rather than imposing a fixed column count.
principles.example: CSS Grid Layout shipping in major browsers, 2017

movements.name: Material Design
movements.summary: Google's system of paper-like surfaces with real shadows and meaningful motion, later personalised (Material You, 2021) and made more emotional (Expressive, 2025).

principles.name: Material is the metaphor
principles.idea: A single invented physical material (sheets of paper with thickness) gives consistent rules for depth, shadow and stacking without imitating any real object.
principles.example: Material Design guidelines, Google I/O, 2014

principles.name: Motion provides meaning
principles.idea: Transitions show where things came from and where they went; animation is explanation, not decoration.
principles.example: Android 5.0 Lollipop ripple and shared-element transitions, 2014

principles.name: Bold, graphic, intentional
principles.idea: Print-design grids, baseline, scale and saturated colour drive hierarchy.
principles.example: Material Design 2014 spec with 8dp grid and Roboto type scale

principles.name: Personal by default
principles.idea: Colour is extracted from the user's wallpaper so the system adapts to the person, not the brand.
principles.example: Material You dynamic colour, Android 12, 2021

principles.name: Expressive and tested
principles.idea: Shape, size, colour and springy motion are dialled up to evoke emotion, with each choice validated by research.
principles.example: Material 3 Expressive, 46 studies with over 18,000 participants, 2025

movements.name: Design systems
movements.summary: The corporate standards manual rebuilt as living code: tokens, components and documentation maintained by a team as a product.

principles.name: Systems, not pages
principles.idea: Design reusable components that compose into any page instead of designing pages one by one.
principles.example: Brad Frost, Atomic Design blog post, 2013

principles.name: Tokens as the single source
principles.idea: Colour, spacing and type become named variables shared by design tools and code, so a change propagates everywhere.
principles.example: Salesforce Lightning Design System, 2015

principles.name: The system is a product
principles.idea: A dedicated team versions, documents and supports the system, with adoption as its success metric.
principles.example: Shopify Polaris, released 2017

principles.name: Defaults democratise
principles.idea: A free, good-enough kit lets non-designers ship coherent UI, at the cost of sameness.
principles.example: Twitter Bootstrap, 2011

principles.name: Shared canvas
principles.idea: Libraries live in a multiplayer design tool so the source of truth is collaborative and in the browser.
principles.example: Figma public release, 2016

movements.name: Neubrutalism
movements.summary: A deliberate roughness against polished system UI: thick black outlines, hard offset shadows, flat clashing colour and visible structure.

principles.name: Show the structure
principles.idea: Borders, boxes and the grid are drawn, not hidden; the page admits it is made of rectangles.
principles.example: brutalistwebsites.com, Pascal Deville, by 2015

principles.name: Hard shadow, no blur
principles.idea: Depth is a solid offset block (often black, a few pixels down-right), a printmaker's shadow rather than a renderer's.
principles.example: Neobrutalist UI patterns surveyed by NN/g, 2025

principles.name: Clash on purpose
principles.idea: Two or three saturated flat colours against black and white, chosen to be loud rather than harmonious.
principles.example: Gumroad storefront and dashboard, cited by NN/g, 2025

principles.name: Anti-polish as voice
principles.idea: Roughness signals independence from big-tech sameness and suits creator and indie brands.
principles.example: Figma brand refresh, cited by NN/g, 2025

movements.name: Liquid Glass
movements.summary: Apple's 2025 cross-platform material: real-time refracting, reflecting translucent controls floating over content, praised as craft and criticised for legibility.

principles.name: A digital material
principles.idea: Controls are made of one simulated substance with optical behaviour (lensing, specular highlights) rendered live by the GPU.
principles.example: Liquid Glass announcement, WWDC, 9 June 2025

principles.name: Controls float above content
principles.idea: Navigation is a separate functional layer of floating capsules that shrink on scroll, rather than bars pinned to the screen edge.
principles.example: iOS 26 tab bar that collapses while scrolling in Apple Music, 2025

principles.name: Concentricity
principles.idea: Corner radii of controls nest inside the radii of windows and the hardware itself, so software echoes the device's shape.
principles.example: macOS Tahoe 26 windows and toolbars, 2025

principles.name: One language across devices
principles.idea: The same material and rules span phone, tablet, desktop, watch, TV and headset.
principles.example: iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS Tahoe 26, watchOS 26, tvOS 26, visionOS 26, 2025

keyWorks.title: Liquid Glass (iOS 26, macOS Tahoe 26 and siblings)
Liquid Glass Is Cracked, and Usability Suffers in iOS 26 (NN/g)
Liquid Glass revision with transparency control (iOS 27)

movements.name: Generative AI design
movements.summary: Images, interfaces and code produced from natural-language prompts; the designer shifts from making artefacts to directing, curating and constraining a model.

principles.name: Describe, then select
principles.idea: The designer writes intent in words and curates among many outputs; taste and editing replace drawing as the core act.
principles.example: Midjourney open beta via Discord, July 2022

principles.name: Conversation as interface
principles.idea: A text box and a thread replace menus; the command line returns, but in natural language.
principles.example: ChatGPT, 30 November 2022

principles.name: Latent style
principles.idea: Every historical style is addressable by name, so pastiche is instant and originality must come from the brief and the edit.
principles.example: Jason Allen, Théâtre D'opéra Spatial, made with Midjourney, Colorado State Fair, 2022

principles.name: Prompt to product
principles.idea: Working interfaces and code are generated from a description and refined by feedback, collapsing design and build.
principles.example: Andrej Karpathy coins 'vibe coding', February 2025

principles.name: The system constrains the model
principles.idea: Design systems become the guardrails (tokens, components) that keep generated UI on-brand and usable.
principles.example: Figma Make, Config, May 2025

figures.name: Douglas Engelbart
figures.summary: Led SRI's Augmentation Research Center and gave the 1968 demo that introduced the mouse, windows, hypertext and real-time collaboration.

principles.name: Augment, don't automate
principles.idea: Computers should amplify human intellect and collective problem-solving, not replace people.
principles.example: Augmenting Human Intellect: A Conceptual Framework, 1962

principles.name: Co-evolve tools and people
principles.idea: Skills, methods and tools must develop together; a tool that demands learning is acceptable if it raises the ceiling.
principles.example: NLS chord keyset plus mouse, demonstrated 1968

principles.name: Bootstrapping
principles.idea: Use the system to build the system, so improvements compound.
principles.example: ARC team developing NLS inside NLS, late 1960s

keyWorks.title: Augmenting Human Intellect: A Conceptual Framework
NLS demonstration ('The Mother of All Demos')

figures.name: Alan Kay
figures.summary: Conceived the Dynabook and led the Smalltalk work at Xerox PARC that produced overlapping windows and the modern desktop.

principles.name: The computer is a medium
principles.idea: A personal computer is a new medium for thought and expression, like print, not a calculator.
principles.example: Alan Kay and Adele Goldberg, Personal Dynamic Media, 1977

principles.name: Doing with images makes symbols
principles.idea: Interfaces should move from action (mouse) to imagery (icons, windows) to symbols (code), following how children learn.
principles.example: Smalltalk environment on the Xerox Alto, 1970s

principles.name: Design for children of all ages
principles.idea: If a child can author on it, the system is truly general; learnability is the test of power.
principles.example: A Personal Computer for Children of All Ages (Dynabook), 1972

keyWorks.title: A Personal Computer for Children of All Ages (Dynabook)

figures.name: Larry Tesler
figures.summary: At PARC and Apple he championed modeless interaction and, with Tim Mott, cut, copy and paste.

principles.name: No modes
principles.idea: A key or click should always do the same thing; hidden modes are the main source of user error.
principles.example: Gypsy editor, with Tim Mott, 1975

principles.name: Conservation of complexity
principles.idea: Every application has irreducible complexity; the question is whether the user or the designer absorbs it.
principles.example: Tesler's Law, articulated at Apple in the 1980s

principles.name: Test with real users
principles.idea: Watch non-programmers use the system and change the design to fit them.
principles.example: Gypsy, built for and tested with editors at Xerox's publishing subsidiary Ginn & Co., 1975

figures.name: Jef Raskin
figures.summary: Conceived the Macintosh project in 1979 as an inexpensive appliance and later codified humane interface design.

principles.name: The information appliance
principles.idea: A computer should be a single-purpose-feeling appliance, ready to use without configuration.
principles.example: Canon Cat, 1987

principles.name: Design for habit
principles.idea: Users form habits; interfaces must be monotonous (one way to do a thing) and modeless so habits never betray them.
principles.example: The Humane Interface, 2000

figures.name: Bill Atkinson
figures.summary: Wrote QuickDraw, MacPaint and HyperCard, inventing the menu bar, marching ants, the lasso and fast round rectangles.

principles.name: Speed is a design property
principles.idea: An interface only feels direct if drawing is instant; performance engineering is interface design.
principles.example: QuickDraw RoundRects, May 1981

principles.name: Tools you can see working
principles.idea: Selection and editing are made visible (marching ants, FatBits zoom) so the user always knows the state.
principles.example: MacPaint, 1984

principles.name: Authoring for everyone
principles.idea: Give non-programmers cards, buttons and a simple script so they build their own software.
principles.example: HyperCard, 1987

figures.name: Susan Kare
figures.summary: Drew the original Macintosh icons and bitmap typefaces on graph paper, setting the visual grammar of the personal computer.

principles.name: Icons as road signs
principles.idea: An icon must be read instantly at small size, so reduce to the one silhouette that carries the meaning.
principles.example: Macintosh Trash, Paintbrush and Scissors icons, 1984

principles.name: Meaning in a 32-by-32 grid
principles.idea: Every pixel is a decision; constraint produces clarity and a hand-made warmth.
principles.example: Kare's graph-paper icon notebooks, 1983, acquired by MoMA in 2015

principles.name: Wit makes the machine human
principles.idea: A small joke or face (a smiling computer, a dogcow) makes software feel friendly rather than clerical.
principles.example: Happy Mac startup icon, 1984

figures.name: Bruce Tognazzini
figures.summary: Apple's first applications engineer; wrote the first Apple Human Interface Guidelines and later partnered in Nielsen Norman Group.

principles.name: The guideline as contract
principles.idea: Consistency across applications is a promise to users, so write it down and enforce it.
principles.example: Apple Human Interface Guidelines, first edition (Apple II), 1978

principles.name: Fitts's law at the edge
principles.idea: Targets at the screen edge are effectively infinite in depth, so put the most-used commands there.
principles.example: The Macintosh menu bar pinned to the top edge, 1984

principles.name: First principles over fashion
principles.idea: Ground interaction in durable principles (anticipation, latency reduction, visible state) rather than look.
principles.example: Tog on Interface, 1992

keyWorks.title: Human Interface Guidelines: The Apple Desktop Interface

figures.name: Steve Jobs
figures.summary: Apple and NeXT co-founder who acted as the decisive patron of interface design, from the Macintosh through Aqua to the iPhone.

principles.name: Look at the world
principles.idea: Ground interface forms in everyday objects; if the world is full of a shape, the screen should be able to draw it.
principles.example: Insisting on QuickDraw round rectangles, May 1981

principles.name: Typography belongs in computing
principles.idea: Proportional, beautiful type is a requirement, not a luxury, traced by Jobs to a calligraphy class.
principles.example: Macintosh proportional bitmap fonts, 1984

principles.name: Integrate and edit
principles.idea: Own hardware and software together and cut ruthlessly so the product feels like one thing.
principles.example: iPhone with multi-touch and no hardware keyboard, 2007

figures.name: Muriel Cooper
figures.role: Book designer, digital design researcher, educator
figures.summary: MIT Press design director turned founder of the Visible Language Workshop, whose 1994 Information Landscapes put typography into navigable 3D space.

principles.name: Information as landscape
principles.idea: Hierarchy can be spatial depth and focus rather than page order; the reader flies through text.
principles.example: Information Landscapes, TED5, 1994

principles.name: Designers must build the tools
principles.idea: If design moves onto screens, designers have to work inside the computer, not hand off to engineers.
principles.example: Visible Language Workshop, MIT, from the mid-1970s

principles.name: Modernist rigour, radical variation
principles.idea: Bauhaus discipline can be pushed into new forms rather than repeated.
principles.example: Learning from Las Vegas, first edition design, MIT Press, 1972

figures.name: Jony Ive
figures.summary: Apple's industrial design chief from the iMac to the iPhone, who took over software design and led the flat redesign of iOS 7.

principles.name: Simplicity is order
principles.idea: Simplicity is not absence of ornament but bringing order to complexity.

principles.name: Deference to content
principles.idea: The interface should step back so content and the user's task lead.
principles.example: iOS 7 translucent bars and borderless buttons, 2013

principles.name: Materials lead form
principles.idea: Form follows how a material is worked (polycarbonate, aluminium unibody, glass).
principles.example: iMac G3 translucent Bondi Blue polycarbonate, 1998

figures.name: Scott Forstall
figures.summary: Led iPhone software from its creation until 2012 and was widely reported as the leading internal advocate of skeuomorphic iOS.

principles.name: Familiarity first
principles.idea: New users on a new device learn faster when apps look like the objects they replace.
principles.example: iPhone OS 1.0 Notes, Calculator and Clock apps, 2007

principles.name: The platform is the product
principles.idea: Open the device to third-party apps under shared rules and frameworks.
principles.example: iPhone SDK and App Store, 2008

figures.name: John Maeda
figures.summary: MIT Media Lab professor, RISD president and tech-industry design executive who argued designers must code and later that they must understand AI.

principles.name: Learn the material by coding
principles.idea: Designers should write simple programs to understand the computer as a medium.
principles.example: Design By Numbers, 1999

principles.name: Laws of simplicity
principles.idea: Reduce, organise, save time; simplicity is subtracting the obvious and adding the meaningful.
principles.example: The Laws of Simplicity, 2006

principles.name: Computational design as a business force
principles.idea: Track design's shift into technology companies and name computational design as its own category.
principles.example: Design in Tech Report, 2015

figures.name: Joshua Davis
figures.summary: Flash-era designer whose praystation.com won the 2001 Golden Nica and who opened his source files to a generation.

principles.name: Program the composition
principles.idea: Write rules and let randomness compose within them; the output is a family, not a single image.
principles.example: praystation.com experiments, 2001

principles.name: Give away the source
principles.idea: Publishing working files builds a community that learns and remixes.
principles.example: praystation.com, one of the first sites to publish its Flash source files, 2001

figures.name: Yugo Nakamura
figures.summary: Tokyo designer trained in engineering whose physics-driven Flash interfaces and UNIQLOCK defined interactive craft in the 2000s.

principles.name: Behaviour modelled on nature
principles.idea: Use the maths of natural motion (springs, growth, flow) so interaction feels familiar without instruction.
principles.example: ecotonoha for NEC, 2004

principles.name: Loop as experience
principles.idea: A perpetual, music-timed loop turns a utility (a clock) into a brand ritual.
principles.example: UNIQLOCK for Uniqlo, 2007

figures.name: Matías Duarte
figures.summary: Designed Danger's Sidekick and Palm's webOS, then led Android and Material Design at Google.

principles.name: Cards for multitasking
principles.idea: Running apps as physical-feeling cards you flick away makes concurrency graspable.
principles.example: Palm webOS card view, 2009

principles.name: A material, not an imitation
principles.idea: Invent one consistent material with its own physics instead of copying leather and wood.
principles.example: Material Design, 2014

principles.name: Between literal and abstract
principles.idea: Avoid both heavy skeuomorphism and austere signage; Android's Holo was framed against both.
principles.example: Android 4.0 Ice Cream Sandwich Holo, 2011

figures.name: Albert Shum
figures.summary: Led the Microsoft design team behind Windows Phone 7, the first mass-market phone interface built on Metro's typographic flatness.

principles.name: Authentically digital
principles.idea: Drop simulated materials; let typography, colour and motion native to the screen do the work.
principles.example: Windows Phone 7, 2010

principles.name: Signage, not simulation
principles.idea: Borrow from transit wayfinding: big type, flat colour fields, immediate legibility.
principles.example: Windows Phone 7 Live Tiles, 2010

figures.name: Loren Brichter
figures.summary: Independent developer who invented pull-to-refresh and whose flat, colour-coded Letterpress anticipated iOS 7.

principles.name: The gesture is the button
principles.idea: Fold a command into the natural motion of the content so no control is needed.
principles.example: Pull-to-refresh in Tweetie 2, 2009

principles.name: Colour as state
principles.idea: Flat fields of colour can encode game state and ownership more clearly than texture.
principles.example: Letterpress, 2012

figures.name: Ethan Marcotte
figures.summary: Coined 'responsive web design' in 2010 and defined it as fluid grids, flexible images and media queries.

principles.name: One design, many facets
principles.idea: Treat every device as a facet of a single experience rather than building separate sites.
principles.example: Responsive Web Design, A List Apart, 2010

principles.name: Proportion over pixels
principles.idea: Express the grid as ratios (target over context equals result) so layout scales.
principles.example: Responsive Web Design (book), 2011

principles.name: Learn from architecture
principles.idea: Borrow responsive architecture's idea that structure and inhabitant shape each other.
principles.example: Responsive Web Design, A List Apart, 2010

keyWorks.title: The Boston Globe website (with Filament Group)

figures.name: Brad Frost
figures.summary: Wrote Atomic Design (2013 post, 2016 book), the most influential method for building interface design systems.

principles.name: Atoms to pages
principles.idea: Build interfaces from atoms, molecules, organisms, templates and pages, moving between abstract parts and concrete screens.
principles.example: Atomic Design blog post, 10 June 2013

principles.name: A living pattern library
principles.idea: Keep the components in a working, browsable environment that is the real code, not a static PDF.
principles.example: Pattern Lab, 2013

principles.name: Maintain it like a product
principles.idea: A design system needs people, process and governance to survive past launch.
principles.example: Atomic Design (book), 2016

figures.name: Alan Dye
figures.summary: Head of Apple's Human Interface design from 2015, who led Liquid Glass before leaving for Meta in December 2025.

principles.name: Interface as material
principles.idea: Treat UI as a physical material with its own optics and behaviour, not as flat graphics.
principles.example: Liquid Glass, 2025

principles.name: Hardware and software as one shape
principles.idea: Let the interface adopt and even disguise the hardware's form.
principles.example: Dynamic Island, iPhone 14 Pro, 2022

figures.name: Bret Victor
figures.summary: Former Apple human-interface inventor whose essays and talks argue for immediate, explorable, physical computing; founder of Dynamicland.

principles.name: Immediate connection
principles.idea: Creators need to see the effect of every change instantly; latency between thought and result kills ideas.
principles.example: Inventing on Principle, talk, 2012

principles.name: Information software is graphic design
principles.idea: Most software is for learning, not doing, so its core problem is showing data, not adding interaction.
principles.example: Magic Ink, essay, 2006

principles.name: Beyond pictures under glass
principles.idea: Hands do far more than tap glass; the future interface should use the body and physical space.
principles.example: A Brief Rant on the Future of Interaction Design, 2011

keyWorks.title: A Brief Rant on the Future of Interaction Design

events.label: Sketchpad
events.note: Ivan Sutherland's light-pen drawing program introduced direct graphical manipulation and constraints, the seed of CAD and of every drawing tool since.

events.label: The Mother of All Demos
events.note: Engelbart's 9 December demo showed the mouse, windows, hypertext and live collaboration in one system.

events.label: Dynabook proposal
events.note: Alan Kay's paper imagined a personal, portable computer for learning, a blueprint for the laptop and tablet.

events.label: Xerox Alto
events.note: The first workstation with a bitmapped display, mouse and graphical interface, built at PARC.

events.label: Apple visits Xerox PARC
events.note: Jobs and Apple engineers saw the Alto's interface, which shaped the Lisa and Macintosh.

events.label: Xerox Star 8010
events.note: The first commercial computer sold with a desktop of icons, folders and a mouse.

events.label: Apple Lisa
events.note: The first mass-market GUI computer, launched 19 January at US$9,995.

events.label: Apple Macintosh
events.note: Launched 24 January with Kare's icons and proportional fonts, bringing the GUI and desktop publishing to individuals.

events.label: Microsoft Windows 1.0
events.note: Started the path by which the GUI reached most of the world's PCs.

events.label: HyperCard
events.note: Bill Atkinson's card-and-button authoring tool prefigured the web and no-code design tools.

events.label: NeXT Computer
events.note: Jobs's workstation with Display PostScript and the Dock; its OS became the foundation of Mac OS X and iOS.

events.label: World Wide Web goes public
events.note: Tim Berners-Lee's hypertext system, built on a NeXT, made the link the basic unit of screen design.

events.label: NCSA Mosaic
events.note: The first popular browser to show images inline with text, turning web pages into graphic layouts.

events.label: Information Landscapes at TED5
events.note: Muriel Cooper's last demo showed typography moving in 3D space, a lost path for interface design.

events.label: Windows 95
events.note: The Start menu and taskbar fixed the desktop paradigm for a mass audience.

events.label: CSS Level 1
events.note: The W3C's 17 December recommendation separated presentation from structure, making web typography and layout designable.

events.label: Macromedia Flash 1.0
events.note: A vector animation plug-in that let designers make the web move for a decade.

events.label: iMac G3
events.note: Translucent Bondi Blue plastic made consumer computing playful and set the Y2K look.

events.label: Aqua unveiled
events.note: Apple's glossy, translucent Mac OS X interface opened a decade of rich, rendered UI.

events.label: Processing
events.note: Reas and Fry's sketchbook language made code an everyday material for designers and artists.

events.label: CSS Zen Garden
events.note: One HTML file restyled by many designers proved CSS could carry real visual design.

events.label: iPhone
events.note: Announced 9 January: multi-touch glass replaced keys, and skeuomorphic rendering stood in for touch.

events.label: App Store
events.note: Third-party apps turned interface design into a mass profession and a visual arms race.

events.label: iPad
events.note: Announced 27 January; its bookshelf and leather apps marked skeuomorphism's high-water mark.

events.label: Windows Phone 7 and Metro
events.note: Microsoft's typographic, flat phone interface brought Swiss principles to mobile.

events.label: Responsive Web Design
events.note: Ethan Marcotte's A List Apart article named fluid, device-agnostic layout.

events.label: Thoughts on Flash
events.note: Jobs's open letter explained why iOS would not run Flash, ending the Flash era's momentum.

events.label: Bootstrap
events.note: Twitter's open-source UI kit made a shared component system the default starting point of the web.

events.label: Forstall leaves Apple
events.note: His October departure put Jony Ive in charge of software design and ended Apple's skeuomorphic era.

events.label: iOS 7
events.note: Announced 10 June, Apple's flat redesign made Swiss-derived minimalism the industry default.

events.label: Atomic Design
events.note: Brad Frost's post gave design systems a shared vocabulary of components.

events.label: Material Design
events.note: Announced 25 June at Google I/O, the first publicly documented, cross-platform design language at Google's scale.

events.label: Figma public release
events.note: A multiplayer, browser-based design tool made shared component libraries the working medium.

events.label: Fluent Design System
events.note: Microsoft added light, depth and translucent Acrylic to Metro's flatness.

events.label: Flash end of life
events.note: Adobe ended Flash Player support on 31 December, closing the era formally.

events.label: Glassmorphism and macOS Big Sur
events.note: Michal Malewicz named the frosted-glass trend as Big Sur shipped translucent, depth-rich UI.

events.label: Material You
events.note: Google's dynamic colour derived from the user's wallpaper made personalisation a system property.

events.label: Midjourney open beta
events.note: Opened 12 July via Discord, putting text-to-image generation in designers' hands.

events.label: ChatGPT
events.note: Released 30 November, it made conversation a mainstream interface and triggered the AI design era.

events.label: Apple Vision Pro
events.note: Released 2 February; visionOS's glass windows were the direct ancestor of Liquid Glass.

events.label: Vibe coding
events.note: Andrej Karpathy's February coinage named prompt-driven software making; Collins Word of the Year 2025.

events.label: Material 3 Expressive
events.note: Google's most researched update reintroduced emotion, shape and springy motion to Material.

events.label: Liquid Glass
events.note: Announced 9 June at WWDC, Apple's first cross-platform redesign since iOS 7, met with mixed-to-negative reviews.

events.label: Alan Dye leaves Apple for Meta
events.note: Apple's human-interface chief departed in December, months after shipping Liquid Glass.

events.label: Liquid Glass revised at WWDC 2026
events.note: Apple reduced default transparency and added a clear-to-tinted slider, a rare public course correction.
